paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent chooses actions, but the action actually carried out can differ from its choice. This paper studies how to learn policies that account for that uncertainty while pursuing reward. It connects the problem to disturbances in robotics, such as sudden external forces.

The authors formalize two different robustness criteria. In the first, an adversary replaces the chosen action with a specified probability. In the second, an adversary adds a perturbation to an action in a continuous action space. These formulations distinguish occasional action replacement from interference with the selected action itself. The paper proposes algorithms for tabular problems and extends the approach to deep reinforcement learning.

Experiments across MuJoCo domains show robust policies and improved performance even when perturbations are absent. That second finding suggests that training against action uncertainty can also help ordinary performance. The authors interpret this as evidence that action robustness can act as implicit regularization; the experiments support that interpretation without establishing a universal benefit.
icml-2019-action-robust-reinforcement-le.tldr: Two formulations of adversarial action uncertainty produce robust reinforcement learning policies and improve unperturbed performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Neural networks usually learn representations within an architecture chosen beforehand, while decision trees learn a branching structure over features supplied beforehand. Adaptive neural trees combine these capabilities: the model learns useful representations and develops a tree architecture from the training data.

Representation learning appears throughout the tree, including its edges, routing functions, and leaves. A training algorithm based on backpropagation grows the architecture using basic modules such as convolutional layers. This makes architectural growth part of learning, allowing the resulting model to adapt to the size and complexity of the dataset. Conditional computation also enables lightweight inference by making computation depend on how an input is routed.

The reported classification and regression results are competitive, alongside benefits in computational efficiency and feature organization. The learned hierarchy can separate concepts relevant to prediction, including associations such as natural versus manufactured objects. The contribution therefore concerns both predictive performance and the organization of the model: its structure can reflect useful distinctions in the data.
icml-2019-adaptive-neural-trees-40b28422.tldr: Adaptive neural trees jointly learn representations and grow branching architectures, combining competitive prediction with conditional computation and meaningful feature hierarchies.

paragraphs: Training deep classifiers can require substantial labeling effort and computation. This paper addresses the problem of learning effectively from a small labeled dataset by bringing together two approaches that use available resources differently: active learning and data augmentation.

Active learning selects informative examples from an unlabeled collection for an oracle to label. Data augmentation creates additional training examples artificially. Each has a weakness identified by the authors: augmentation can spend computation generating examples that are not informative, while active learning may select too few examples to adequately support training. The proposed Bayesian generative active learning approach combines selection and augmentation to address these complementary concerns.

The paper provides theoretical and empirical evidence for more efficient training and better classification than the augmentation and active learning approaches considered. Experiments cover MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. The findings support combining decisions about which examples deserve labels with the generation of additional training data, rather than treating those resource decisions as unrelated parts of training.
icml-2019-bayesian-generative-active-dee.tldr: A Bayesian approach combines active learning and data augmentation, with theoretical and experimental evidence for more efficient training and better classification.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can make classification examples confusing. This paper introduces a loss function that lets a deep neural network abstain during training. The resulting deep abstaining classifier can avoid committing on confusing samples while continuing to improve its predictions on the samples it does classify.

The role of abstention depends on the kind of noise. When unreliable labels or confusing examples correlate with features of the data, abstention supports learning representations of those features. When label noise is arbitrary, the classifier can instead serve as a data cleaner by identifying examples likely to have incorrect labels. These are distinct uses of the same training mechanism, rather than a claim that all noisy examples share a recognizable pattern.

The authors also analyze the loss function to support adjusting abstention rates as learning progresses. Image classification experiments demonstrate usefulness under different noise types. For arbitrary label noise, the paper reports significant improvements over previously published results on multiple benchmarks, supporting abstention as an effective training tool in those settings.
icml-2019-combating-label-noise-in-deep-.tldr: Allowing neural networks to abstain during training helps them learn with unreliable labels and identify likely mislabeled examples.

paragraphs: This paper develops new concentration inequalities for conditional value at risk, or CVaR. The contribution concerns how tightly this risk quantity can be bounded. The authors compare their lower and upper bounds with an established earlier result, assessing both mathematical improvement and its significance in empirical comparisons.

For the lower bound, the conclusion is especially strong: the authors analytically establish that their bound is strictly tighter than the earlier one. Their empirical results also indicate that the difference is significant. These two pieces of evidence serve different purposes. The analysis establishes the ordering of the bounds, while the experiments show that the improvement can be consequential in the cases examined.

The upper bound has a qualified result. It can be looser in some cases, although empirical comparisons show significantly tighter bounds in most cases studied. The paper discusses when each upper bound is preferable. Its overall empirical conclusion is that both new bounds will often be substantially tighter, without claiming uniform superiority for the upper bound.
icml-2019-concentration-inequalities-for.tldr: New CVaR concentration bounds include a provably tighter lower bound and an upper bound that is often, but not always, tighter empirically.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders learn compact latent representations of high dimensional data. Their usual assumption that observations are independent means they optimize distributions for individual examples without accounting for correlations between them. This paper addresses datasets where relationships between examples are known beforehand and may matter for the representations being learned.

Correlated variational autoencoders incorporate those relationships through a prior based on the correlation structure. That change makes inference intractable, so the authors develop an approximation using an undirected graph of the relationships. They average tractable lower bounds associated with all maximal acyclic subgraphs. In this way, simpler graph structures provide manageable pieces for approximating the objective involving the correlated prior.

The experiments evaluate matching and link prediction on public rating benchmarks, along with spectral clustering on synthetic data. The reported results show effectiveness relative to baseline algorithms. The contribution is a way to make known relationships between examples participate in representation learning, together with an approximation that addresses the computational difficulty those relationships introduce.
icml-2019-correlated-variational-auto-en.tldr: Correlated variational autoencoders incorporate known relationships between examples through a structured prior and a tractable approximation to the resulting objective.

paragraphs: DeepNose investigates whether neural networks can learn useful representations of odorant molecules directly from their three dimensional structures. The work is motivated by the hypothesis that odorant receptors can be viewed as three dimensional convolutional filters that extract molecular features. This hypothesis guides the model design without itself establishing how biological receptors operate.

The authors first train a convolutional autoencoder to compress molecular structures into a lower dimensional representation. They then test whether the learned features predict physical properties and human odor perceptions using molecular structure alone. This separates learning a representation of chemical space from evaluating whether that representation contains information useful for predicting properties and perceptions.

The learned features often outperform molecular descriptors used in computational chemistry, despite being learned without human expertise supplying those features. The result supports learning predictive chemical features directly from structure. The authors further propose that DeepNose could help predict other bioactivities and understand factors shaping ensembles of odorant receptors; these are proposed implications of the approach.
icml-2019-deepnose-using-artificial-neur.tldr: DeepNose learns features from three dimensional molecular structures that often outperform established descriptors in predicting physical properties and human odor perceptions.

paragraphs: Multiple time series can contain shared patterns without every series following the same structure. This paper develops a Gaussian process model that learns covariance structure across selected groups of series. Its aim is to use shared information while preserving differences in which components apply to each series.

The model places an Indian Buffet Process prior on the presence of shared kernels. This supports a selective decomposition of covariance structure, with parameters shared across the series that use a particular component. The authors also investigate whether the models remain well defined when infinitely many latent components are introduced. A practical search algorithm explores a larger space of possible structures efficiently.

Experiments on five real datasets show improvements over existing methods in both discovering structure and making predictions. Those findings support the usefulness of selective sharing: relationships across series can inform a model without requiring a single covariance structure for the entire collection. The contribution combines a model for discovering shared components with a search procedure for finding useful compositions.
icml-2019-discovering-latent-covariance-.tldr: A Gaussian process model selectively shares covariance components across time series, improving structure discovery and prediction on five real datasets.

paragraphs: Graph representations can support prediction while still failing to identify precisely which structures matter for a particular task across the graph. This paper introduces Ego-CNNs to address that gap. The goal is to learn representations that help detect task relevant structures and make those structures available for explanation or discovery.

The model uses ego convolutions at each layer and stacks those layers in an egocentric manner. It can be trained jointly with the model performing the task, tying structure detection to the predictive objective. The authors also connect Ego-CNNs with convolutional network visualization techniques, allowing the detected structures to be illustrated rather than remaining only implicit in a learned representation.

Experiments report task performance comparable to leading graph embedding models, along with effective visualization and efficient operation. Incorporating scale free priors, which the authors associate with social network data, can further improve training efficiency. The stated benefit is therefore a combination of competitive prediction, more precise structure detection, and tools for examining what the model has found.
icml-2019-distributed-egocentric-represe.tldr: Ego-CNNs learn graph representations that detect and visualize task relevant structures while achieving competitive predictive performance.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient training requires workers to exchange gradient information, making communication a potential bottleneck. Compression reduces the information sent, and error compensation can improve convergence when compression is used. This paper studies that combination in a communication pattern that matches parameter server systems.

In this setting, compression happens twice: workers compress their local gradients before sending them to a server, and the server compresses the aggregated gradient before returning it. An analysis of a single broadcast pass does not capture both stages. DoubleSqueeze analyzes error compensation at the workers and at the server, directly addressing the errors introduced along this two stage communication path.

The theoretical results establish compatibility with arbitrary compression techniques, improved convergence rates over noncompensated approaches such as quantized and sparse SGD, and linear speedup with the number of workers. An empirical study validates the theoretical findings. The contribution makes error compensated compression applicable to the full communication cycle of a parameter server, rather than analyzing only one part of that cycle.
icml-2019-doublesqueeze-parallel-stochas.tldr: DoubleSqueeze analyzes error compensated gradient compression at both workers and a parameter server, establishing improved convergence and linear worker speedup.

paragraphs: The success of AlphaGo and its successors demonstrated the strength of deep reinforcement learning in Go, but questions about understanding and using these methods remained for researchers. ELF OpenGo addresses that problem through an open reimplementation of AlphaZero, making a strong Go system available as a subject and tool for research.

The system demonstrates superhuman performance with a 20–0 record against leading professional players. This establishes that the released approach is capable of exceptionally strong play in the reported evaluation. The authors also use the implementation for extensive ablation studies, examining the system to investigate phenomena arising during model training and during the inference procedures used for gameplay.

The research contribution includes both the functioning system and the opportunity to study it. Code, trained models, self play datasets, and auxiliary data are publicly available. These resources give the research community access to materials underlying the work, while the analyses explore questions that headline playing strength alone does not resolve about training and gameplay behavior.
icml-2019-elf-opengo-an-analysis-and-ope.tldr: ELF OpenGo openly reimplements AlphaZero, demonstrates superhuman Go performance, and provides analyses and resources for studying training and gameplay.

paragraphs: This paper considers settings where using sensitive attributes, such as gender or ethnicity, can be acceptable. It argues that assigning different models to different groups should serve each group's interests. The proposed approach trains separate classifiers while imposing preference guarantees grounded in doing good and avoiding harm.

The guarantees involve two comparisons. Rationality requires a majority of individuals in each group to prefer their assigned classifier to a pooled classifier that ignores group membership. Envy freeness requires that majority to prefer its assigned classifier to the classifier assigned to any other group. These are majority based guarantees within groups; they do not assert that every individual benefits.

A recursive procedure adaptively chooses which group attributes to use when separating classifiers. The authors provide formal conditions for preference guarantees in terms of generalization error. On real datasets, the procedure improves accuracy while maintaining the guarantees on test data. The findings support evaluating group specific modeling through explicit comparisons with both pooled and alternative group models.
icml-2019-fairness-without-harm-decouple.tldr: Group specific classifiers improve accuracy in the reported tests while satisfying majority preference guarantees against pooled and other groups' models.

paragraphs: Recovering a signal becomes difficult when its measurements have been subsampled or rearranged, leaving their correspondence uncertain. This paper introduces homomorphic sensing as an abstraction of problems such as unlabeled sensing and shuffled linear regression. It asks when a transformed observation still uniquely identifies the original signal.

The theoretical setting consists of a known linear subspace and a finite collection of linear transformations. The authors develop algebraic conditions guaranteeing that a point in the subspace is uniquely determined by its image under some transformation from that collection. The framework recovers established conditions for unlabeled sensing while also producing new results and extensions.

The paper also presents two algorithms based on dynamic programming for unlabeled sensing in small dimensions. One combines dynamic programming with branch and bound. Applied to image registration under affine transformations, that algorithm matches or exceeds leading methods on benchmark datasets. The work thus connects conditions for unique recovery with algorithms, while explicitly locating the unlabeled sensing solutions in the small dimensional setting.
icml-2019-homomorphic-sensing-c91f18e57b.tldr: Homomorphic sensing gives algebraic guarantees for recovering signals under uncertain linear transformations and algorithms for small dimensional unlabeled sensing.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what clustering by kernel normalized cut approaches at the population level. The distinction matters because a clustering computed from observed data is a finite sample object, whereas a population criterion describes the underlying distribution. The authors establish a mathematical connection between these two levels.

Their first result is a nonasymptotic upper bound on the expected distortion rate. From it, they show convergence to population weighted k-means in a particular reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The next result identifies that population weighted k-means problem with population normalized cut. Combining the results shows that kernel normalized cut converges to the population normalized cut solution.

This chain of results gives a population interpretation to the clustering procedure, rather than only describing its behavior on a particular dataset. The population objective can be understood through the indivisibility of the underlying distribution, a criterion relevant to theoretical analyses of spectral clustering. The authors present the results as a source of insight into normalized cut and spectral clustering behavior.
icml-2019-kernel-normalized-cut-a-theore.tldr: The paper proves that kernel normalized cut converges to its population counterpart through a connection with weighted k-means in a kernel space.

paragraphs: Multivariate Hawkes processes model discrete events occurring across multiple streams. This paper studies learning their causal structure when the streams are not correctly aligned in time. The problem is relevant to inference from observations whose timing differs from the underlying event process because of unknown delays.

The authors formalize synchronization noise by giving each dimension's event stream a random, unknown time shift. This is a specific observation model: uncertainty concerns the alignment of streams. They characterize how robust the classical maximum likelihood estimator is to this noise and introduce a new approach for recovering causal structure when synchronization noise is present.

Experiments show accurate recovery across a wide range of noise levels and substantial improvements over classical estimation methods. These findings support explicitly addressing timing misalignment when learning relationships between event streams. The contribution includes both an analysis of an established estimator under the proposed noise model and a learning approach whose reported empirical performance remains strong across the tested noise levels.
icml-2019-learning-hawkes-processes-unde.tldr: A new method recovers Hawkes process causal structure under unknown time shifts, outperforming classical estimators across tested noise levels.

paragraphs: Generalized linear models offer an interpretable way to relate many covariates to an outcome. When the number of covariates is large relative to the number of observations, uncertainty becomes an important part of inference. Bayesian methods quantify that uncertainty, but the paper identifies roughly cubic runtime in parameter dimension as a major computational obstacle.

LR-GLM reduces time and memory requirements by approximating the data with a lower rank representation. Combined with either a Laplace approximation or Markov chain Monte Carlo, it produces an approximation to the full Bayesian posterior. The reported runtime reduction is a full factor of the parameter dimension, making the computational savings directly relevant to high dimensional problems.

The authors rigorously analyze approximation quality and show how rank controls a tradeoff between computational cost and statistical accuracy. Experiments support the theory and demonstrate effectiveness on large real datasets. The central contribution is therefore a tunable way to reduce the cost of uncertainty quantification, with theoretical support for the approximation being introduced.
icml-2019-lr-glm-high-dimensional-bayesi.tldr: LR-GLM uses low rank data approximations to accelerate Bayesian inference in generalized linear models with a tunable computational–statistical tradeoff.

paragraphs: A standard generative adversarial network produces samples using its generator, even though training also creates a discriminator. This paper proposes using both components during sampling. The Metropolis-Hastings GAN combines ideas from Markov chain Monte Carlo with GANs to improve the samples obtained from an already trained generator.

The method builds a wrapper around the generator using the discriminator from training. As a result, samples come from a distribution implicitly defined by the pair, rather than only the generator's distribution. The paper gives a strong conditional result: with a perfect discriminator, the wrapped generator samples exactly from the true data distribution even if the generator is imperfect. The perfect discriminator condition is essential to the stated exactness claim.

Experiments demonstrate sampling benefits on multiple benchmarks, including CIFAR-10 and CelebA, using DCGAN, WGAN, and progressive GAN models. These results support the practical value of retaining the discriminator for sample generation. The broader contribution is to make the learned discriminator part of the sampling procedure itself.
icml-2019-metropolis-hastings-generative.tldr: MH-GAN uses a trained discriminator to improve generator sampling, with exact recovery of the data distribution conditional on a perfect discriminator.

paragraphs: Comparing structured objects requires accounting for both their features and their internal relationships. This paper treats objects such as undirected graphs as probability distributions in a metric space and introduces a transportation distance that combines those two sources of information.

The proposed Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance minimizes a transport cost while jointly exploiting features and structure. In the paper's comparison, Wasserstein focuses on feature information, while Gromov-Wasserstein focuses on structural information. Combining them provides a geometry for structured objects that reflects both what their parts are like and how those parts relate. The authors discuss the resulting distance's properties and computational aspects.

On a graph classification task, the method outperforms the graph kernels and deep graph convolutional networks considered. The paper also uses its metric properties to explore graph barycenters and Fréchet means in a clustering setting. These examples show that the distance supports more than pairwise comparison: it also provides a framework for discussing representative or average graphs within groups.
icml-2019-optimal-transport-for-structur.tldr: Fused Gromov-Wasserstein compares graphs using both features and structure, supporting classification and geometric notions of representative graphs.

paragraphs: Programming languages can express complex conditions, but probabilistic inference methods cannot readily condition models on many of them. Predicate exchange addresses this mismatch by turning hard predicates into soft ones. Instead of only stating whether a condition holds, a soft predicate measures how consistent the model's variable values are with that condition.

The method substitutes this soft predicate for the likelihood term in a Bayesian posterior. It then uses a variant of replica exchange Markov chain Monte Carlo to draw posterior samples. This connects declarative conditions to a sampling procedure: the condition becomes a graded measure that participates directly in inference rather than remaining only a test applied to values.

The authors implement predicate exchange as a language independent tool that executes probabilistic programs in a nonstandard way. They demonstrate the approach on health sequence models and inverse rendering. The contribution is a mechanism for bringing a broader class of programmatically expressed knowledge into probabilistic inference, together with demonstrations in two different modeling settings.
icml-2019-predicate-exchange-inference-w.tldr: Predicate exchange softens programmatic conditions and uses replica exchange sampling to incorporate a broader class of declarative knowledge into probabilistic inference.

paragraphs: This paper proposes improved estimation of covariance and precision matrices using developments in random matrix theory. Its starting point is progress in estimating distances between covariance matrices. The authors turn that progress into a method for matrix estimation across a broad family of metrics.

The breadth of the metric family matters because the proposal is not tied to a single way of judging an estimate. The paper reports that the method substantially outperforms the sample covariance estimate and competes with leading alternatives. It also reports simpler and faster computation. The stated result therefore combines estimation quality with computational practicality, rather than presenting accuracy as the only criterion for comparing methods.

Applications to linear and quadratic discriminant analysis show significant gains as well. These downstream results provide evidence that the estimation improvements can benefit statistical machine learning tasks, beyond comparisons of the matrices themselves. The authors describe this as suggesting practical interest, supported by the combination of competitive estimation, lower computational burden, and improvements in the reported classification applications.
icml-2019-random-matrix-improved-covaria.tldr: Random matrix theory supports covariance and precision estimates that combine competitive accuracy with simpler computation and gains in discriminant analysis.

paragraphs: When analysis concerns only recent data, a sliding window provides a formal way to specify which observations count. This paper studies how to estimate heavy hitters within such a window while preserving differential privacy. Its central question is the cost of privacy when the relevant data continually changes as the window advances.

For a window containing w observations, earlier work had additive error proportional to w with a fixed positive proportionality constant. The proposed efficient algorithm achieves additive error of order w to the three quarters power, up to logarithmic factors. It uses space of order the square root of w, again up to logarithmic factors. Both stated quantities grow sublinearly with the window size.

The result improves the dependence of estimation error on window size while also keeping memory below linear growth. This addresses accuracy and storage together for private analysis of recent observations. The contribution is an algorithmic guarantee for heavy hitters in the sliding window setting, rather than a reported empirical comparison.
icml-2019-sublinear-space-private-algori.tldr: A private sliding window heavy hitter algorithm achieves roughly w^(3/4) additive error using roughly square-root-of-w space, up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can benefit from recognizing that different actions are related. Act2Vec learns context based vector representations of actions so that similar actions can be grouped and their relationships used by a learning algorithm. The aim is to make action relationships part of the information available for learning.

The framework extracts prior knowledge of an environment from demonstrations and incorporates it into action vectors that encode compatible behavior. Those representations are then used in two ways: to augment state representations and to improve approximation of Q-values. This gives the learned action structure a role both in representing the agent's situation and in estimating the value of its choices.

The authors visualize and test the embeddings in a drawing task, a high dimensional navigation task, and StarCraft II, which supplies a large action space setting. The work presents action representations as a means of improving reinforcement learning performance through relationships between actions. Its demonstrations across these domains examine the usefulness of that representation strategy in different kinds of decision problems.
icml-2019-the-natural-language-of-action.tldr: Act2Vec learns action embeddings from demonstrations and uses action relationships to enrich state representations and improve Q-value approximation.

paragraphs: Variational inference makes posterior inference manageable by turning it into optimization over a parameterized approximation. That optimization can become difficult when different variational parameters control variables that the model strongly correlates. This paper studies how the choice of optimization direction can account for those relationships.

Traditional natural gradients use information from the variational approximation. The authors identify a problem when that approximation differs from the true posterior: its natural gradient can fail to correct for the relevant correlations. Their Variational Predictive Natural Gradient instead accounts for relationships between model parameters and variational parameters. The change broadens the information used to determine how optimization should move.

A simple example illustrates the underlying insight. The paper also demonstrates empirical value in classification, deep generative modeling of images, and probabilistic matrix factorization for recommendation. These examples support the usefulness of the proposed gradient across different latent variable applications. The contribution targets optimization difficulties arising from correlations that the current variational approximation does not adequately capture.
icml-2019-the-variational-predictive-nat.tldr: The Variational Predictive Natural Gradient accounts for relationships between model and variational parameters to address correlation related optimization difficulties.

paragraphs: Reusing experience across reinforcement learning environments can reduce the need to gather everything anew. This paper studies reuse in policy search, where the relevant samples are entire trajectories. That creates a more complex transfer problem than moving individual state, action, next state, and reward observations between value based learners.

The authors use multiple importance sampling to construct robust gradient estimators for trajectories collected in environments with different transition models. They also introduce several variance reduction techniques. Together, these methods address both how transferred trajectories contribute to policy updates and how to make the resulting estimates less variable.

The theoretical guarantee against negative transfer applies when the transition models are known. For unknown models, the paper proposes efficient estimation methods in two specified settings: the target task belongs to a finite candidate set, or it belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Empirical results demonstrate the estimators' effectiveness. The contribution therefore pairs trajectory reuse with a conditional robustness result and methods for handling particular forms of model uncertainty.
icml-2019-transfer-of-samples-in-policy-.tldr: Multiple importance sampling enables trajectory reuse across environments, with robustness against negative transfer established when transition models are known.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks can synthesize data without specifying an explicit likelihood function. This paper investigates why likelihood information can nevertheless help train them. Its goal is to provide theoretical grounding for attempts to stabilize and improve GAN training that had largely relied on empirical heuristics.

The authors draw on variational theory for diffusion processes to derive a regularization scheme based on likelihoods. This connects a mathematical perspective on stochastic processes with a concrete modification to GAN training. They also introduce an approach for training a GAN from an unnormalized distribution instead of empirical samples, changing the form in which the target distribution can be supplied.

Experiments provide evidence that the theoretically motivated algorithms improve on the practices considered. The contribution is both explanatory and methodological: it clarifies theoretical roots of likelihood based training ideas while deriving new training procedures. The reported improvements support those procedures empirically, and the unnormalized distribution approach broadens the training setting examined beyond learning directly from a collection of observed examples.
icml-2019-variational-annealing-of-gans-.tldr: Variational diffusion theory motivates likelihood based GAN regularization and a method for training from unnormalized distributions, with experimental evidence of improvement.
